> **Where we got to (Wednesday).** We adapted the Study A question
> ("did the community shift from pre to post, and differently by arm?") to our
> dataset. Study B has no pre and post — each person was sampled once — so the
> question becomes: do pill, injectable and ring differ in community
> composition? Next: decide whether the Bray-Curtis or the Jaccard result is
> the one we show, and write the "what we do not believe" slide.

```{r setup}
# Load the usual libraries.
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(phyloseq)   # holds the count data + sample table together
library(microViz)   # pipes for ordination on phyloseq objects
library(vegan)      # PERMANOVA (adonis2)
library(patchwork)  # puts several ggplots side by side

source(here("R/count_tables.R"))

# Build the phyloseq object from the MICROBIOME table, applying the filter our
# group agreed in the QC report: keep only species seen (at least 1 read) in
# at least 5 people.
ps <- as_counts(dataset = "group_b", table = "microbiome",
                min_count = 1, min_samples = 5)

# SAFETY CHECK: the count columns must be in the same order as the metadata
# rows. DESeq2 and the distance code will not warn if they are not — they will
# just be wrong. as_counts() does the ordering for us; we prove it here.
stopifnot(identical(colnames(otu_table(ps)), rownames(sample_data(ps))))
cat("Species kept after filtering:", ntaxa(ps), "\n")
cat("Samples:", nsamples(ps), "\n")
```

## The study, in two sentences

93 women use one of three contraceptive methods — the pill (28), an
injectable (39) or the vaginal ring (26) — and each gave one vaginal swab.
Nobody was randomised to a method, so the arms may differ in other ways too
(that is the caveat we carry through the whole analysis).

## Step 1 — Ordination: does a picture separate the arms?

```{r ordination}
# Library size (total reads per person), added to the metadata BEFORE the
# ordination so we can colour points by it. Points far apart only because one
# person had few reads would be a red flag for Bray-Curtis.
sample_data(ps)$depth <- sample_sums(ps)

# microViz pipeline: transform (none — Bray-Curtis uses raw counts directly),
# then distances between samples, then PCoA, then plot coloured by arm.
ord_bray <- ps |>
  tax_transform("identity") |>
  dist_calc("bray") |>
  ord_calc("PCoA")

p_arm <- ord_plot(ord_bray, colour = "arm") +
  labs(title = "Coloured by arm", colour = "Arm") +
  theme_classic()
p_bv <- ord_plot(ord_bray, colour = "bv") +
  labs(title = "Coloured by BV (Amsel)", colour = "BV") +
  theme_classic()
p_nugent <- ord_plot(ord_bray, colour = "nugent") +
  labs(title = "Coloured by Nugent score", colour = "Nugent") +
  scale_colour_viridis_c() +
  theme_classic()

p_depth <- ord_plot(ord_bray, colour = "depth") +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(title = "Coloured by library size (log10)", colour = "Reads") +
  theme_classic()

(p_arm | p_bv) / (p_nugent | p_depth)
```

**Read the plot:** the axis titles show how much of the variation each axis
holds. Colour by library size is our check that depth is not driving the
picture. BV and Nugent score are clinical measures of the same disruption the
community itself shows — if they line up with an axis, that axis is "BV-ness",
and we must then ask whether the arms differ in BV for a reason other than the
method.

## Step 2 — PERMANOVA: is the pattern bigger than chance?

PERMANOVA asks one plain question: if you shuffle the arm labels at random,
how often do you get between-arm differences in community composition *this*
large? A small p-value means the real labelling produces a difference you
would rarely see by chance. The R² says what share of the between-sample
variation is explained by the grouping. A link to read more:
Anderson (2001), *Austral Ecology* 26:32–46 —
<https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1442-9993.2001.01070.x>.

```{r permanova-arm}
# Pull the sample table out and match it to the distance matrix order.
meta <- as(sample_data(ps), "data.frame")

# The distance matrix, reused for every test below so all tests see the same
# geometry. Set a seed so the permutation p-value is reproducible.
dist_bray <- phyloseq::distance(ps, method = "bray")
set.seed(123)

adonis2(dist_bray ~ arm, data = meta, permutations = 999)
```

```{r permanova-adjusted}
# No randomisation: arms may differ in BV status, pH or Nugent score, and any
# of those could produce a community difference on its own. Putting them in
# the same model means the arm row asks: "does the method matter OVER AND
# ABOVE these?" by="margin" reports each variable with all the others already
# accounted for, so no variable gets credit for a neighbour's work.
set.seed(123)
adonis2(dist_bray ~ bv + nugent + ph + arm, data = meta,
        permutations = 999, by = "margin")
```

```{r permanova-jaccard}
# Robustness check: Bray-Curtis uses how MUCH of each species is there;
# Jaccard only uses WHICH species are present (presence/absence). If the arm
# effect survives both, it is not just an abundance-depth artefact.
dist_jac <- phyloseq::distance(ps, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE)
set.seed(123)
adonis2(dist_jac ~ arm, data = meta, permutations = 999)
```

## Step 3 — Which pairs of arms differ?

The overall test only says "somewhere among the three arms". With 93 samples
in three groups, each pairwise test is small, so read these as
under-powered, not as "no difference".

```{r pairwise}
# A distance "matrix" in R is stored as a flat list of pairs, so to cut out
# only the rows and columns of two arms we first unfold it into a real matrix.
dist_mat <- as.matrix(dist_bray)

pairs <- list(c("pill", "injectable"), c("pill", "ring"), c("injectable", "ring"))
results <- map_dfr(pairs, function(arms) {
  keep <- meta$arm %in% arms
  set.seed(123)
  fit <- adonis2(as.dist(dist_mat[keep, keep]) ~ arm, data = meta[keep, ],
                 permutations = 999)
  tibble(arm1 = arms[1], arm2 = arms[2],
         n1 = sum(meta$arm == arms[1]), n2 = sum(meta$arm == arms[2]),
         R2 = round(fit$R2[1], 3), p_value = fit$`Pr(>F)`[1])
})
# Three tests means three chances to be wrong by luck; multiply each p by 3
# (Bonferroni) so the family-wide error stays at 5%.
results |>
  mutate(p_bonferroni = pmin(p_value * 3, 1)) |>
  gt::gt()
```

## What we found, in plain words

- On its own, **arm explains only about 3% of the community variation and it
  is not significant** (p = 0.11). The ordination picture agrees: the three
  arms overlap heavily.
- The clinical measures matter more. Together the BV/Nugent/pH model explains
  about 29% of the variation; on its own BV is significant (p = 0.03).
- Arm *after* accounting for the clinical measures: R² = 0.028, p = 0.07 —
  close to the line, but not over it, and the marginal test is the most
  generous one we ran.
- The pairwise tests hint that **pill vs injectable** may differ
  (p = 0.027, R² = 0.038), but after correcting for doing three tests the
  p-value is 0.081 — we cannot claim it with 67 samples.
- The honest headline: with 93 people and no randomisation, this analysis
  does **not** detect a method effect. It does not prove there is none —
  small samples can only find big effects.

## Choices made

- Tested the Study B card question "do the three methods differ in community
  composition?" because Study B has no pre/post time points; the Study A
  wording was not runnable on this data.
- Filtered species to those seen in at least 5 people (min_count = 1,
  min_samples = 5), following the QC report's flagged candidates; the
  alternative of no filtering would let rare noise species into the distances.
- Bray-Curtis on raw counts as the primary distance; alternatives considered:
  Jaccard (added as a robustness check) and Aitchison/CLR-Euclidean (not run).
- PERMANOVA with 999 permutations, fixed seed 123; alternative: 99
  permutations (less stable p-values).
- Adjusted model tests arm *after* bv, nugent and ph, rather than testing arm
  alone and interpreting it as a method effect.
- Pairwise tests use Bonferroni ×3; alternative: report unadjusted p-values
  (would overstate significance).
- No samples dropped; library size checked visually in the ordination rather
  than by dropping low-read samples.
